issues.legal_issue: A village panchayat cannot validly gift common land to a trust when the governing statute restricts the power to gift that land to specified beneficiaries.
material_facts: The land in question was shamlat land vested in the Gram Panchayat.
The Gram Panchayat resolved to gift land to a trust for a dispensary and for a college and polytechnic, and the State Government approved the proposals subject to conditions.
The trust was not among the beneficiaries to whom the Act permitted gifts of shamlat land.
The State relied on Rule 13, which permitted gifts for certain public purposes with prior government approval.
issues.conclusion: The statutory restrictions in Sections 5A and 5B controlled the power to gift the land; Rule 13 could not enlarge that power. The resolutions, approvals, and gift deeds were void ab initio, and the land was to be returned for use by the Gram Panchayat.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 5 and 5A of the Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act govern the use of vested shamlat land and permit gifts only to the specified classes of beneficiaries; Section 5B addresses transfers contrary to the prescribed conditions. Section 15(2)(ff) authorises rules concerning gifts to those specified beneficiaries, not gifts to others. A rule cannot override its parent Act, so Rule 13 of the Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Rules, 1964 could not authorise gifts prohibited by the Act. Rules 3 and 6 also prescribe requirements for use or leasing of shamlat land, which were not followed.

predicates.public_interest_writ_challenges_transfer: A public-interest writ proceeding challenges a transfer of village common land.
predicates.land_is_village_common_land: The transferred land is common village land vested in a village panchayat.
predicates.land_is_gifted_to_ineligible_recipient: The panchayat gifts the land to a recipient outside the classes eligible to receive such a gift.

issues.definition: When a public-interest writ challenges a gift of panchayat-vested common land to an ineligible recipient, the gift is void and the land is restored to the village.

issues.legal_issue: Land treated as forest cannot be transferred for a non-forest purpose without prior central approval, and a transfer subject to release from the Forest Department cannot proceed before that release.
material_facts: The revenue records showed the gifted land as occupied by the Forest Department, and the State Government’s approvals expressly required the land to be released from that department through the proper channel.
The land had not been released before the gift deeds were executed.
No prior approval of the Central Government for using the land for a non-forest purpose was shown.
The State argued that the land’s forest status had expired, but its own approval condition and affidavits acknowledged the need for release from the Forest Department.
issues.conclusion: The land’s forest status attracted the Forest Conservation Act regardless of ownership or classification, and the gifts made without release and required central approval were invalid.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2 of the Forest Conservation Act, 1980 prohibits a State Government or authority from directing that forest land be used for a non-forest purpose or assigned to a private person without prior approval of the Central Government. In T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad v. Union of India, the Court held that “forest” includes land understood as forest in its dictionary sense and land recorded as forest in government records, regardless of ownership or classification.

predicates.land_is_recorded_or_used_as_forest: Government records or the land’s use show that the land is forest land.
predicates.land_is_transferred_for_nonforest_use: An authority transfers the land or permits its use for a purpose other than forestry.
predicates.prior_central_approval_is_absent: The required central approval was not obtained before the transfer or change of use.

issues.definition: When land recorded or used as forest is transferred for a non-forest purpose without prior central approval, the transfer is invalid.

issues.legal_issue: A trust has no right to retain village or other public land that was never validly transferred to it, and land held without a valid transfer must be restored to its owner.
material_facts: A Gram Panchayat resolution proposed transferring about 17 acres to the trust, but the proposal was never approved by the State Government.
The trust’s positions about its interest in and possession of that land were inconsistent, and it ultimately acknowledged that the Panchayat could take back land not approved for transfer.
The trust stated that it had no interest in or possession of 500 acres given for afforestation; that land had not been transferred to it by an approved gift.
The trust had also occupied land belonging to the Border Security Force, but the land was returned to that force during the proceedings.
issues.conclusion: The trust had no right or interest in the approximately 17 acres and had to return it to the Gram Panchayat. The 500 acres taken into State possession were to be delivered to the Gram Panchayat and used consistently with forest law; the Border Security Force land had already been restored to its owner.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that a proposed transfer without the required approval confers no right on the proposed recipient. Public land held without a valid transfer remains subject to the rights of its owner and must be restored. The Court also directed that the afforested land be used consistently with the Forest Conservation Act.

predicates.public_interest_writ_challenges_public_l: A public-interest writ proceeding challenges a person’s occupation of public land.
predicates.public_land_is_occupied_without_valid_tr: The occupant holds public land without a completed, valid transfer from its owner.

issues.definition: When a public-interest writ establishes that public land is occupied without a valid transfer, the land is restored to its owner.

issues.legal_issue: Invalidating a land transfer does not entitle the recipient to retain the land because it built structures on it, although the assessed value of those structures may be paid to the recipient.
material_facts: The Court held the gifts of the land to the trust invalid and directed that possession be returned to the Gram Panchayat.
The trust had constructed buildings on the land and relied on its construction expenditure as a reason not to be divested of possession.
The Court directed the State to assess the construction costs using the trust’s account books and to pay the assessed amount, with the amount recoverable from the Gram Panchayat.
issues.conclusion: The trust could not retain the land because of its construction, but the State was directed to pay the assessed value of the buildings and recover that payment from the Gram Panchayat.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated the construction expenditure as a matter of remedial compensation, not as a basis for validating the void transfer or allowing the recipient to keep the land. The assessed cost was to be determined from the recipient’s account books; the judgment cited no earlier case or separate statutory provision for this direction.

predicates.public_interest_writ_establishes_invalid: A public-interest writ proceeding results in a finding that the transfer of the land was invalid.
predicates.recipient_built_structures_on_the_land: The recipient constructed buildings on the land before it was required to give possession back.

issues.definition: When an invalid land transfer is set aside and the recipient has built structures on the land, the recipient may receive the assessed construction value but does not retain the land.
